subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident
passage:
“Omkar, why is everyone heading toward the old bridge?” Mohit asked, dragging a suitcase.
“The message said the highway is closed and the bridge road is the safe route. I forwarded it to the building group.”
“The bridge road is flooded already! My cousin just called. The shelter is the other way, behind the school.”
“What? But it said official—”
“Who sent it to you?”
“Some forward. It had a lot of exclamation marks.” His face fell. “Oh no. Mrs Nair took her whole family that way.”
“Come on, call her, tell everyone to turn back.”
Later that night, in the shelter, Omkar opened the district office page and read the real map, twice. “Next time I check before I send.”
“Good,” Mohit said. “Save this page.”

qa.q: Where is the shelter, according to Mohit?
qa.a: The shelter is the other way, behind the school.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he learned the bridge road was flooded?
qa.a: He felt alarmed and guilty, as his face fell and he worried about Mrs Nair's family.

qa.q: What could Omkar do before sharing a warning next time, and why?
qa.a: He could check the district office page or another official source first, because a forward with wrong routes can send neighbours toward danger.

qa.q: How did the forwarded message affect Mrs Nair's family?
qa.a: They headed for the bridge road, which was already flooded, and had to be called and told to turn back.

grounding: After a cyclone warning, a teen forwards a message with wrong evacuation routes, confuses neighbours and later learns to check official sources.

subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident
passage:
When the cyclone warning came for our coast last year, I did something I'm still embarrassed about. I'm Chandrika. A message landed in our building's group: “URGENT evacuation route: take Beach Road to the college shelter.” It had a map, lots of red, and “forward to everyone”. It looked official. I forwarded it to four groups within a minute.
It was wrong. Beach Road was the one road the district office had closed, and the college wasn't a shelter that year. Francis Uncle from the second floor packed his elderly mother into an auto and headed for Beach Road. Police turned them back at the barrier, and they lost almost an hour in the rain reaching the right shelter at the school.
Later I found the real route on the district office's page in two minutes. Two minutes I hadn't spent.
Now, before I forward anything in an emergency, I check the official page or the radio first. If I can't check it, I don't send it.

qa.q: How many groups did Chandrika forward the message to?
How does Chandrika feel looking back on forwarding it?
qa.a: Chandrika still feels embarrassed, knowing two minutes of checking could have spared Francis Uncle an hour in the rain.

qa.q: What rule does Chandrika follow now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Check the official page or the radio before forwarding in an emergency, so only confirmed routes spread.

qa.q: What was the evening like for Francis Uncle?
qa.a: Francis Uncle, with his elderly mother in an auto, was turned back at the barrier and lost almost an hour in the rain.

grounding: Shows a student forwarding a viral message with a wrong cyclone evacuation route, confusing a neighbour, and learning to check official sources first.

subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident
passage:
Class teacher's note, after the cyclone holiday
On the evening of the warning I saw it happen in our class parents' group. Dolma, whose mother had added her to the group, forwarded a message saying the cyclone would hit at 2 am and that everyone near the market should go to the old bus stand. It carried no source.
Within twenty minutes, Lavanya's mother wrote that she was packing to leave. The old bus stand was low-lying; the district office's actual shelter was the high school. I posted the official page link and asked everyone to follow only that.
When school reopened, Dolma came to me before assembly, very quiet. She said she'd thought she was helping. We looked together at how to find the district office's updates and the weather department's page, and what a source line looks like.
Dolma asked if she could explain this to the class herself. I have said yes, for Friday.

qa.q: Where was the district office's actual shelter?
How did Dolma seem when she came to the teacher before assembly?
qa.a: Dolma seemed very quiet and ashamed, having thought the message was helping.

qa.q: What should Dolma check before forwarding an emergency message next time?
qa.a: Whether it has a clear source and matches the district office or weather department page; if not, it shouldn't be sent.

qa.q: How was the warning evening for Lavanya's mother?
qa.a: Lavanya's mother began packing to go to a low-lying spot, frightened and confused until the official link was posted.

grounding: A teacher notes a student forwarding an unsourced cyclone message that confuses a classmate's family, and later learning to check official sources before sharing.
